content.title: About
content.content: Pickled celery consists of celery stalks that have been brined with vinegar, spices, and sometimes sugar. It has a crisp texture and a mildly sour, aromatic flavor that makes it a popular ingredient in salads, appetizers, and Asian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Celery belongs to the Apiaceae family and is closely related to parsley and dill.
Pickling retains most of the B‑vitamins and minerals such as potassium and folate.
In Russia, pickled celery is often served as a snack with vodka.
Celery contains phthalides, compounds that may help lower blood pressure.
Celery stalks can be used as a natural flavoring in cocktails.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Celery provides flavonoids and vitamin C, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Nitrate compounds in celery may promote vessel dilation and reduce blood pressure.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and contributes to a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium assists in fluid balance and muscle function.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C and other phytonutrients help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to celery, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Pickled celery often contains a lot of salt, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Large amounts may cause gas and discomfort in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Vinegar content
items.content: Vinegar can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled celery is used in salads, sandwiches, sushi rolls, as a garnish for meat or fish, and even in cocktails. Slice it into thin rounds or strips and serve as a snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated in its original brine in a sealed jar. When stored properly, it stays fresh for 3–4 weeks. Discard if mold appears or an off‑odor develops.

content.title: About
content.content: Congee is a traditional Asian rice porridge cooked by simmering rice for a long time until it reaches a creamy consistency. The vegetable version includes carrots, broccoli, peas and other seasonal vegetables, making the dish nutritious and balanced.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Congee is often served in hospitals and rehabilitation centers because of its easy digestibility.
In China congee is considered a "comfort food" that helps recovery after illness.
Traditionally the rice for congee is rinsed several times to remove excess starch.
Vegetables can be fresh or frozen, which simplifies preparation.
In Japan a similar soup is called "okayu" and is frequently served with pieces of fish.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The soft texture and high hydration level make congee suitable for people with digestive issues.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice and vegetables provide vitamin B1, B3 and B6, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Vegetables add dietary fiber, promoting regular bowel movements.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The dish fits low‑fat diets as the main calorie source is carbohydrates.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C from the vegetables enhances the body’s defense mechanisms.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to rice, experiencing skin reactions or gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If soy sauce or broth is added, the dish can become high in sodium, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Bacterial growth risk
items.content: Leaving congee at room temperature for more than 2 hours can allow bacterial growth; it should be refrigerated promptly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot congee with vegetables, optionally drizzle soy sauce, sesame oil, or sprinkle chopped green onions. For extra protein, add boiled chicken breast or tofu.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the prepared congee and store it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. When reheating, add a little water or broth to restore the creamy consistency.

content.title: About
content.content: Whiting (Merlangius merlangus), also known as picarel, is a marine fish of the cod family that inhabits the coastal waters of the Atlantic Ocean and the North Sea. It has a light, firm flesh with a mild flavor, low fat content and high protein levels.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whiting can change its skin colour to blend with the surrounding water, becoming paler in open sea.
In Europe, whiting is a traditional ingredient in fish‑and‑chips and other classic dishes.
Wild individuals may reach up to 70 cm and over 3 kg, but most commercial catches are 30–45 cm long.
The species migrates seasonally, moving to warmer coastal waters in summer for spawning.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Whiting provides about 18 g of high‑quality protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The fish contains very little saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, which are essential for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Whiting is a source of selenium, iodine and phosphorus, nutrients that support immune function and thyroid health.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Although lower than in oily fish, whiting still provides modest amounts of EPA and DHA, beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, including whiting.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Coastal fish can accumulate mercury and cadmium; choose products from reputable suppliers.

items.title: Food poisoning
items.content: Improper storage or insufficient cooking can allow bacterial growth leading to foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Whiting can be baked, boiled, pan‑fried or steamed. It is often breaded and fried to a golden crust. The mild flesh pairs well with lemon, fresh herbs (parsley, dill) and light sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh fillets should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C and used within 2 days. Frozen whiting can be stored at –18 °C for 3‑4 months. Before cooking, check the smell: it should be clean, sea‑like, without a strong ammonia odor.

pasta-with-cream-sauce-meat-and-added-ve.title: Pasta with Cream Sauce, Meat, and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with cream sauce, meat and vegetables is a dish of boiled pasta tossed in a smooth cream sauce, combined with sautéed meat (usually beef or chicken) and a mix of vegetables such as broccoli, carrots, bell pepper and zucchini. The dish balances the richness of the sauce, the heartiness of the meat and the freshness of the vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cream sauce is often made from heavy cream, butter and Parmesan cheese, giving it a distinctive aroma.
Pasta is traditionally cooked al dente so it retains a slight bite and does not become mushy in the sauce.
Adding vegetables boosts the vitamin and fiber content, making the meal more balanced.
In Italy similar dishes are called "pasta al forno" where the ingredients are baked, creating a golden crust.
Meat can be swapped for plant‑based alternatives such as soy crumble for a vegetarian version.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Meat and pasta provide a complete set of amino acids that support tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and whole‑grain pasta are rich in B1, B2, B3 and B6 vitamins, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: The cream sauce, especially when cheese is used, supplies calcium important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Fiber and antioxidants
items.content: Vegetables like broccoli and bell pepper add fiber and antioxidants that support digestion and immunity.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: The combination of carbs, fats and protein provides lasting satiety.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The cream sauce and meat make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑watchers.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cream and cheese contain saturated fats, which can affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: People with dairy sensitivities should use plant‑based cream alternatives.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Prepared sauces and cheese can be high in salt; choose low‑sodium options when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, mixing it with the sauce, meat and vegetables. Garnish with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan or a pinch of black pepper for extra flavor. For a different texture, bake the dish in the oven until the top is golden.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. When reheating, add a splash of milk or broth to keep the sauce from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Baked flavored potato chips are thinly sliced potatoes that are cooked in an oven with little to no added oil. They are coated with a variety of seasonings (salt, spices, cheese, barbecue, etc.) and offer a crunchy texture and intense flavor while containing less fat than traditional fried chips.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Baked chips gained popularity in the early 2000s as a healthier alternative to fried snacks.
A "quick‑bake" technology at high temperatures (200‑220 °C) is used to achieve a crisp exterior.
Flavorings can be natural (herbs, spices) or artificial, but must meet food‑safety regulations.
In the United States baked chips are often labeled as "baked" and may contain up to 30 % fewer calories than their fried counterparts.
Some brands add a small amount of olive or sunflower oil to the dough to improve taste and texture.

items.title: Lower fat content
items.content: Compared with traditional fried chips, baked versions contain significantly less total fat, helping to reduce the calorie load of a serving.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Small amounts of vitamin C survive the baking process, providing antioxidant protection.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The potato skin retains dietary fiber that aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: No trans fats
items.content: Unlike some fried snack varieties, baked chips typically do not contain trans fatty acids.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Flavored chips often contain high levels of salt, which can be problematic for individuals with hypertension.

items.title: Allergens in seasonings
items.content: Certain flavor blends may include dairy, gluten, or soy ingredients that can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Still calorie‑dense
items.content: Even with reduced fat, the carbohydrate content keeps the overall calorie count relatively high, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature cooking can produce acrylamide, a potential harmful compound; modern manufacturers aim to keep its levels low.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Baked chips are a convenient snack on their own, can be tossed into salads, used as a crunchy topping for soups, or incorporated into creative dishes such as homemade tacos. Opt for varieties without artificial colorants for a cleaner snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep chips in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from light. Once opened, consume within 1‑2 weeks to maintain crispness and flavor. Discard any chips that develop a stale or rancid odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato chips are thinly sliced potatoes that are deep‑fried until crisp and lightly salted. They are a popular snack worldwide, commonly sold in bags, boxes, or served in fast‑food restaurants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial chip brand appeared in the United States in 1853.
There are more than 300 chip flavors, but the classic version is lightly salted.
Chips can be made from regular or sweet potatoes.
In some countries chips are served with dips such as sour cream, cheese sauce, or barbecue.
Thin slicing and rapid frying help retain much of the fresh potato flavor.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Chips provide carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C content
items.content: A small amount of vitamin C is retained when chips are fried properly, contributing to antioxidant protection.

items.title: Convenient snack
items.content: The crunchy texture and mild saltiness make chips an easy, quick snack.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Consuming too many chips can lead to excess sodium intake, raising the risk of hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Chips are high in fat and calories, so they should be eaten in moderation, especially when weight control is a goal.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may be allergic to potatoes or to additives used during frying.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Frying in certain oils can produce trans fats; choose products fried in refined vegetable oils without hydrogenation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chips are convenient straight from the package, as a side for sandwiches, salads, or dips. They can be briefly reheated in the oven to restore crispness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store chips in a sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, consume within 1–2 weeks to maintain crunch and flavor.
